{{Short description|Theorem in probability theory}}

'''Cramér's  decomposition theorem''' is a result in [[probability theory]]. It is well known that if [[random variable]]s <math>\xi_1</math> and <math>\xi_2</math> are [[independence (probability theory)|independent]] and [[normal distribution|normally distributed]], then their sum is also normally distributed. It turns out that the converse statement is also true. This result was anticipated by [[Paul Lévy (mathematician)|Paul Lévy]] and proved by [[Harald Cramér]].<ref>H. Cramér. Über eine Eigenschaft der normalen Verteilungsfunktion. Math. Z. Vol. 41, no. 1 (1936), 405–414.</ref> As a consequence, a new direction in probability theory emerged—the theory of decompositions of random variables into independent summands (the arithmetic of [[probability distribution]]s<ref>Yu. V. Linnik, I. V. Ostrovskii. ''Decomposition of Random Variables and Vectors''. Transl. Math. Monogr., Vol. 48, American Mathematical Society, Providence, RI, 1977.</ref>).
== Statement of the theorem ==
Let a random variable <math>\xi</math> have a normal distribution and admit a representation as a sum of two independent random variables, <math>\xi=\xi_1+\xi_2</math>. Then the random variables <math>\xi_1</math> and <math>\xi_2</math> are also normally distributed.

The proof of the theorem is based on the theory of [[entire function]]s. It follows from the Cramér decomposition theorem that the normal distribution belongs to the [[Linnik class|Linnik class <math>I_0</math>]].
== Generalizations to locally compact Abelian groups ==

The following theorem gives a complete description of locally compact Abelian groups on which Cramér's decomposition theorem holds.

'''Theorem''',<ref>G. M. Fel'dman. On the decomposition of Gaussian distributions on groups. Theory of Probability and Its Applications, Vol. 22, No. 1 (1977), 133–140.</ref> see also.<ref>G.M. Fel'dman. Arithmetic of probability distributions, and characterization problems on Abelian groups, Transl. Math. Monographs. Vol. 116, Providence, RI: American Mathematical Society, 1993, 223 pp.</ref> Let <math>\xi</math>, <math>\xi_1</math>, and <math>\xi_2</math> be random variables taking values in a second countable locally compact Abelian group <math>X</math>. Suppose that <math>\xi</math> has a [[Gaussian distribution on a locally compact Abelian group|Gaussian distribution]] and that <math>\xi_1</math> and <math>\xi_2</math> are independent. Then the equality <math>\xi=\xi_1+\xi_2</math> implies that <math>\xi_1</math> and <math>\xi_2</math> also have  Gaussian distributions if and only if the group <math>X</math> contains no subgroups topologically isomorphic to the [[circle group]].
